bio.en: Josh Miller is the co-founder and CEO of The Browser Company, the maker of the Arc web browser, and previously led product at TikTok's U.S. operations.
bio.zh: 乔什·米勒（Josh Miller）是 Arc 网页浏览器的开发商 The Browser Company 的联合创始人兼 CEO，此前曾负责 TikTok 美国区的产品业务。

summary.en: Josh explains that the most important hiring criterion is "heartfelt intensity" - people who show up with a fire in their belly and a purpose to prove. He describes how The Browser Company approaches product craft by giving small teams ambitious problems and getting out of their way. The episode explores why a cohort of new, opinionated software companies are rebuilding foundational consumer products from scratch.
summary.zh: 乔什认为，最重要的招聘标准是"发自内心的炽热"——即带着一股冲劲和想要证明自己的目标而来的人。他讲述了 The Browser Company 如何通过把宏大的问题交给小团队、然后不加以干涉的方式来打磨产品工艺。本期还探讨了为何一批富有主张的新兴软件公司正在从零开始重建基础性的消费级产品。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: We want people that show up to our company with some fire in their belly, something that they are out to do. And for each person it's a little bit different. For some people it may be UI Craft details. For other people, it may be achieving double the performance with a quarter of the engineering headcount. Everyone has something, but they show up with this heartfelt intensity. And I think even relative to everything else, I'm going to say, that's it. If you have a team that has heartfelt intensity and is there for a purpose and something to prove, you get it. You give them a very exciting, ambitious product and get out of their way and they will do remarkable work.
turns.zh: 我们希望加入公司的员工都充满激情，怀揣着必达目标的坚定信念。每个人的动机各不相同——对有些人而言，或许是精通UI设计的细节；对另一些人而言，或许是以四分之一的工程团队规模实现双倍的业绩目标。每个人都有自己的专长，但他们都带着真挚的热忱投入工作。相较于其他任何因素，我认为最关键的一点在于：当一个团队心怀热忱、怀揣使命、带着必胜决心时，你就能感受到这种能量。只要赋予他们一个令人兴奋、目标远大的产品，放手让他们自由发挥，他们就能创造非凡的成果。

And, by the way, I'd never been a PM before, so I'm not complimenting myself, I was just learning for the first time. (00:10:36): I mean, you saw me in the previous answer, I'm talking about D5, D7. What's a D5, D7? You can see the graph go up or go down, or stay flat depending on what you want. But what we've found is that optimizing for metrics leaves a lot on the table and it misses a lot. And so, what we do at The Browser Company is we talk about optimizing feelings. How do we want to make someone feel on the other end of our software? Do we want to make them feel joy? Do we want to make them feel fast? Do we want to make them feel organized? Do we want to make them feel focused? What is it the feeling we are trying to evoke in whatever we're doing on a specific project, or a specific feature, or a specific piece of storytelling content? (00:11:31): And I can imagine what's going through the heads of your listeners right now, which is probably a number of things. But among others, that sounds really damn romantic. If they're like, "Okay. You optimizing for feelings." But if you allow me, I would posit that actually this modern way of optimizing for numbers and graphs, especially for what we all do every day, which is make things and put in the world, is what's fairly odd. Because, if you just to yourself daydream about, what are your favorite products or product companies and brands, while it may sound cliche for me, Nike. Nike was one of the first companies that at a very deep level resonate with me as a child. Disney? Disney, same thing. Apple? Before I was a professional in an industry, these were the brands and the products that they made that really made me love something that was ostensibly a commercial product I could buy. But at the moment of creation, at the stage as product people, wondering what should we do, and why, and how? Do they post something? We even had an acronym OBPS. It's like seared into my memory. What is OBPS? And how is it trending over time? Well, I think we should have been asking, and what we at least would ask at The Browser Company and our way of product development is, "Do we think people feel closer to their friends and family?" Or something of that nature? (00:13:52): I think that's what Snapchat got so right. They weren't obsessing about something like, "How many people put an image into the composer and hit the plus button. And the number of times per week means success." They were thinking about something much more human and essential. And so, that is what we've [inaudible 00:14:07] The Browser Company. Don't optimize for metrics, don't optimize for graphs. Use that as a way to keep you honest, and use it as a tool in your toolkit. But fundamentally, none of us are here for that. We're there to make people feel something.
turns.zh:
我只会在这场采访中说一次这个警示。但我想让听众知道，我不相信做事只有一种正确方式。所以，我今天分享的经验，仅适用于我们当下所处的阶段和正在做的事。但我记得自己职业生涯早期时，听过类似的播客节目，并将其奉为圭臬，因为那些成功者创造了令人敬佩的成果。若这听起来像是"自视高人一等"，那绝非本意。这些只是我们发现对自己有效、真正在乎的东西。[00:09:59]。（00:09:58）：好的。我职业生涯早期与现任联合创始人兼CTO赫什共同创立了一家公司。我们有幸让Facebook收购或兼并了这家公司，并在Facebook工作了数年。这是一个卓越的组织，或许是我那个时期见过执行力最强的公司。顺便说一句，我那时从未做过产品经理，所以这并非自夸，只是初次学习。但2014年左右在Facebook的经历，以及至今的观察，让我意识到，硅谷——至少现代版的硅谷——对图表和数据指标的痴迷已到了病态程度。（00:10:36）：比如，我在前面的回答中提到的D5、D7指标。什么是D5、D7？这确实是实现特定目标的极其有效方式，因为数据量化且客观，你能看到曲线上升、下降或持平。但我们发现，过度优化指标会遗漏很多关键信息。于是，我们在The Browser Company推行"优化用户感受"理念。我们思考软件最终用户的体验：想让他们感受到快乐？速度感？条理性？专注力？无论是特定项目、功能模块还是叙事内容，我们都致力于传递特定情感（00:11:31）。我能想象听众此刻的疑惑：这听起来太浪漫了。但请允许我指出，当前以数据和图表为导向的优化方式——尤其是我们日常的工作——才是反常的。回想你最喜欢的品牌或产品，比如耐克、迪士尼、苹果，这些品牌的初代产品都曾以令人惊喜的方式打动了我们，尽管听起来老生常谈。（00:12:29）：你认为沃尔特·迪士尼打造迪士尼乐园时在优化什么？菲尔·奈特设计第一代耐克跑鞋时在想什么？乔布斯构思iPhone或Macintosh时又在畅想什么？诚然，数据是审视自己是否达成目标的绝佳工具。但在创意诞生的那一刻，作为产品设计者，我们更应关注用户的真实感受。
人们总在思考：我们该做什么？为什么要这么做？又该怎么做？我认为，更重要的是，我们要关注人本身——对面那个真实的个体，以及我们真正想让他们感受到怎样的情感。（00:13:10）举个具体例子吧。我加入Facebook时，正值Snapchat势头正盛之际。当时大家都在讨论：我们做得怎么样？该不该担忧？而我们当时的讨论方式是，人们每周在Facebook上分享的次数是多少？他们会发布内容吗？我们甚至还有个缩写词OBPS，至今仍刻在我的记忆里。这是什么意思？它随时间变化的趋势如何？但我认为，我们本该问问自己——至少在The Browser Company，我们在做产品开发时会问：「我们觉得人们是否与亲友的关系更亲近了？」或者类似的问题。（00:13:52）我认为Snapchat就做得非常出色。他们没有执着于『多少人把图片放进编辑器然后点击加号按钮』这类数据，也不以每周的次数来衡量成功。他们更关注人性化和本质层面的东西。这也是我们在The Browser Company的理念：不要为了指标而优化，不要为了图表而优化。把这些当作保持诚实的工具，但从根本上说，我们做这些不是为了数据，而是为了让人们有所感触。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you pointed out, I think a lot of the people are listening are like, "I love that. I wish I could do that. I want to optimize for feelings, but then I got to drive the business forward. I got goals to hit. I want to keep people accountable." I'm curious how you operationalize this approach? How do you actually implement this idea? I imagine you still have goals and metrics and you guys, you talked about retention and things like that.
turns.zh: 正如你所指出的，我觉得很多听众会想：“我喜欢这样做。真希望我能做到这一点。我想以用户体验为导向，但又得推动业务发展。我有目标要达成，还要让团队负责人。” 我很好奇你们是如何将这种方法落地实施的？具体怎么做？我猜你们仍然有目标和指标，而且你们提到了用户留存率之类的问题。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Yeah. Obviously it's difficult to do that in the abstract for another company, and it may not work for every company and every product. But, for example, one of the reasons we found this to be so effective so far is, if you pick the right feeling, it typically tracks pretty closely with the metric you care about. So, for example, we don't have a growth team and we have no semblance of growth projects. However, in many of the new features that we put out into the world, we want people to feel surprise or joy or an emotion like that. Guess what? When people feel that way, they go, "Oh, my God, what was that?" And they start telling their friends and family about it, and they start dropping a screenshot in Slack, et cetera. So, there's one example on the consumer side. I've never built traditional enterprise software selling to CIOs, et cetera. But I can imagine maybe someone in the IT department of a large enterprise wants to feel smart, or wants to feel ahead of the curve or wants to feel secure and ease at what they're doing. (00:15:54): I think sometimes we just forget that whoever your buyer is, or whatever your business objective, at the end of the day we're a bunch of people in a bunch of rooms at the other side of these screens. And just thinking about that person, it could be a buyer, it could be a customer. But I think the truth is the answer to the question Lenny is, when I was earlier in my career, I was searching for the answers or the way to do things, the right, the wrong, the binary. I think anyone that's been doing this or anything for a while learns that it's all nuanced. It's a spectrum. It depends. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. (00:16:26): But I think the true answer, Lenny, is just optimizing for metrics so purely is deeply flawed in my opinion. Optimizing for feelings so purely is flawed as well. And it depends on what you are doing, what the project is and a lot of other things. But I think the reason we come out so strongly is, I do think Silicon Valley has tended so far towards optimizing for graphs and metrics, that if we can reel it back in a little bit, at least as just one company, I think that will be good. But the truth is, it's both. We need to use all the tools we can get, but I think hopefully that's one way that people can operationalize.
turns.zh: 是的。显然，要为其他公司抽象地推行这种方法很困难，也许并非适用于每家公司和每款产品。但比如，我们发现这种方法迄今为止非常有效的一个原因是，如果你选对了用户体验，通常它能与你关心的指标紧密对应。比如，我们没有专门的增长团队，也没有任何类似增长项目的东西。然而，在我们推出的许多新功能中，我们希望用户感受到惊喜、喜悦或类似的情绪。猜猜怎么着？当人们有这种感觉时，他们会说：“天哪，这是什么？” 然后开始跟朋友和家人分享，还会在Slack上分享截图。这只是消费者端的一个例子。我从未开发过面向CIO等企业的传统软件。但我能想象，也许大型企业IT部门的某个人希望感觉自己很聪明、走在前沿、或者在工作中感到安心和轻松。（00:15:54）：我认为有时我们会忘记，无论你的买家是谁，或者你的业务目标是什么，最终我们都是坐在屏幕另一边的房间里的一群人。只要想想那个人，可能是买家，也可能是客户。但我认为事实是，Lenny，回答你的问题时，我职业生涯早期一直在寻找答案或做事的方法，区分对错、非黑即白。但任何做过这件事或任何事情一段时间的人都会明白，一切都是微妙的。这是一个连续体。有些方法有效，有些则不然。（00:16:26）：但我认为真正的答案是，单纯以指标为导向在我看来是存在严重缺陷的。单纯以用户体验为导向同样存在问题。具体取决于你在做什么、项目是什么以及许多其他因素。但我认为我们之所以如此强调这一点，是因为我确实认为硅谷迄今为止一直倾向于以图表和指标为导向，如果我们能稍微收回一点，至少作为一家公司，我认为这会是件好事。但说实话，两者兼顾。我们需要利用所有能用的工具，但我希望这能成为人们操作的一种方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious, just to poke out a little bit, how you actually implement that? So maybe as an example, you recently launched this Peek feature, where you mouse over, I think, a link and it opens up in a little browser that doesn't last. Do you put together a little spec of some sort of, "We're trying to create surprise, and maybe here's a metric we think about it." What's actual day-to-day operational approach to a new feature, in terms of feelings versus metrics?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，具体来说，你们是如何实施的？比如，你们最近推出了Peek功能，用户鼠标悬停在链接上，它会在一个短暂存在的浏览器中打开。你们有没有制定某种规范，写下“我们想创造惊喜，也许这里是我们考虑的指标”之类的内容？对于新功能，从用户体验到指标的日常操作流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Yeah. The truth is I don't think we've operationalized it as formally as we should one day. And we'll probably need to one day. The lucky thing is we are a very tight group of individuals that have now worked together for a long time. So not so formal as there's a PRD at the top of it, we list out the emotions. It's much more, with that project, get Ben in a room and whoever else is working on it and say, "All right. So here's what we're trying to do for people. Here's the problem we're trying to solve or the way we fit in their day. And in that moment people want to feel very light and airy." (00:18:05): So, for the Peek feature [inaudible 00:18:07] he's referencing the use cases. You're on Hacker News and you want to probably in pretty quick succession check out five to seven URLs. And you're not really sure which one you're going to spend time on, but you're going to open a bunch of stuff really quickly. And Peek allows you to effortlessly just peek into it, without leaving Hacker News and context switching to this whole new tab and going back and forth. So in that scenario, the conversation was how do we make it feel really airy and effortless to just whoop, pop it up, pop it back down, lightness, airiness, speed, agility. So again, it's not that we have a, "What is the number one feeling and the number two feeling?" It is much more conversational at this stage, but I am actually really excited. Hopefully we got the privilege one day to have such a large team that we have to figure out a way to do it. So, that's an example of how we think about it.
turns.zh: 是的。说实话，我觉得我们还没有像应该的那样正式地将其流程化。但或许未来我们有必要这么做。幸运的是，我们是一个紧密团结的团队，共同合作已久。虽然没有正式的PRD文档，但我们会列出项目的核心需求。更重要的是，在开发过程中，我们会把团队成员召集起来，讨论项目目标、要解决的痛点，以及如何融入用户的日常生活。比如在Peek功能开发时，我们会让本（Ben）和其他参与者坐在一起，说：“好的，我们要为用户提供这样的体验。这是我们要解决的问题，或者说要如何融入他们的日常生活。”（00:18:05）在设计Peek功能时，他提到了用户场景：用户在Hacker News上快速浏览五到七个网址，但不确定该花时间在哪个页面上。所以他们会同时打开多个页面，而Peek功能让用户无需离开Hacker News就能轻松预览网页，无需切换到新标签页再返回。这种场景下，我们需要思考如何让用户感觉操作顺畅自然，比如一键预览、快速切换、轻便易用、快速高效。当然，我们不会强制规定“第一重要的感觉是什么，第二重要的感觉是什么”，但在现阶段讨论更偏向于交流。不过我真的很兴奋，希望未来我们能有足够大的团队来探索这些可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a good segue to a question I wanted to touch on. So, I asked Scott Belsky what I should ask you. He's a big fan of yours. I don't know if he's an investor? But he's just like, "I love Josh." And asked him, "What should I ask Josh?" And one of his questions was about, you guys ship very quickly. You're shipping meaningful features every Friday. And you also close the loop really well with customers when they come ask for something. You're like, "Hey, here. We did it." What is it that you do, and what can people learn from the way you all operate that allows you to ship quickly?
turns.zh: 这正好引出我想问的一个问题。之前我问斯科特·贝尔斯基（Scott Belsky）该问你什么问题。他是你的忠实粉丝，我不知道他是否是投资者，但他直言：“我超爱乔希（Josh）。”我问他：“该问乔希什么问题呢？”他提到你们团队发布新功能非常迅速，每周五都会上线有意义的功能，而且当用户提出需求时，你们能迅速给出反馈。比如用户说：“嘿，看看这个。”你们就会回应：“好的，我们已经做好了。” 你们是如何做到的，其他团队能从你们的运作方式中学到什么？

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Well, first of all, thank you Scott, if you're listening. It's somewhat of an awkward question admittedly, because it's like someone complimenting you about your product. It's always impossible to really take and accept the compliment, because you see all the blemishes. Of course we see all these ways in which we don't ship fast enough and could be doing a better job listening and building with members. But, at risk of sounding a bit cliche, I really think we ship our values. So, we thought a lot about our values as a company. You can read about them online. And I think if you examine those values and then you look at your compliment or Scott's compliment, you can see [inaudible 00:20:05] one-to-one. So the first, and I really think the most important is, we hire people that show up with heartfelt intensity. (00:20:11): And, a lot of companies I think obsess over craft details. They'll be a value like, "We obsess over the details." What we say is, we want people that show up to our company with some fire in their belly, something that they are out to do. And for each person it's a little bit different. For some people it may be UI Craft details, for other people it may be achieving double the performance with a quarter of the engineering head count. Everyone has something, but they show up with this heartfelt intensity. And I think even relative to everything else, I'm going to say, that's it. If you have a team that has heartfelt intensity and is there for a purpose and something to prove, you give them a very exciting, ambitious prompt and get out of their way and they will do remarkable work. So, showing up with heartfelt intensity. (00:20:54): Our second value is assume you don't know. Assume you don't know. And the value "assume you don't know" is, even if you're a subject matter expert. We have someone in our company that literally built the first version of Chrome and ran it for 16 years. But he more than anyone embodies this beginner's mind of, "I have no idea how this should work or what will happen." And the follow up to that value is, "So we got to get going." It's like dropping in a new city. You just got to walk out the door of your Airbnb turn left and ... Maybe you'll turn right and then you'll hop on the subway, but you just got to get going and see what you find. And so, we have this attitude of, you're showing up with this heartfelt intensity. But you start by saying, "I've no idea what I'm doing. I have no idea what's going to happen." So we've just got to get going. And that biases in a default to action. (00:21:44): We have another value of, start by asking, "What could be?", which is pushing ourselves to be as aspirational, ambitious as possible. So the Peek feature that you mentioned, we just didn't want to solve the problem of context switching. We wanted to almost blur the line between native and web software, and make it feel like a sheet of paper. And really pushing ourselves to be as ambitious as we can be, which is the consequence of blowing back around and more deeply motivating the people working on it. (00:22:13): So, I mean, I could keep going. We have a value, "You're doing it for the crew when you got to swarm. When you got to swarm," and we have value of, "make them feel something." But I think what it all adds up to is, a team that has a lot of heart, has a lot of intrinsic motivation and a, "It's the first day of my career. I wonder what's going to happen?" attitude. And I think all of those things add up to a culture which is, "Let's get something out there. Let's see what happens."
turns.zh:
好的，首先，感谢Scott，如果你在听的话。这确实是个有点尴尬的问题，因为这就像有人在夸赞你的产品一样。人们总是很难真正接受这种赞美，因为你总能看到产品的缺陷。当然，我们也意识到在很多方面做得不够好，比如发货速度不够快，在倾听用户需求和与会员共同成长方面还有提升空间。不过冒着老生常谈的风险，我认为我们真正传递的是我们的价值观。  

我们公司花了大量时间思考我们的价值观，你可以在网上查阅相关内容。我觉得如果你仔细审视这些价值观，再回头看看Scott的赞美，你会发现两者之间有着直接的对应关系。首先，也是最重要的一点是，我们招聘那些带着真诚热情投入工作的员工。（00:20:11）：很多公司过于关注技术细节。他们会宣扬“我们对细节执着到偏执”的价值观。但我们的理念是，我们希望员工带着一股激情加入公司，追求某个目标。每个人的动机各不相同，有些人可能专注于UI细节，有些人则致力于用四分之一的工程团队实现双倍的性能目标。但核心在于，他们都带着真诚的热情投入工作。  

（00:20:54）：我们的第二个价值观是“假设你一无所知”。即使你是个领域专家，我们公司里也有人亲自开发了Chrome的第一个版本并运营了16年。但他最能体现这种初学者心态：“我不知道事情该怎么运作，也不知道会发生什么。” 紧随其后的是：“那我们就开始行动吧。” 这就像初到一座新城市，你只需走出Airbnb的房门，向左转……或许向右转，再搭上地铁，但你就是要行动起来，看看会发现什么。  

（00:21:44）：我们还有一个价值观是“先问‘可以怎样？’”，这推动我们尽可能树立远大志向。就拿你提到的Peek功能来说，我们不想仅仅解决上下文切换的问题，而是想模糊原生应用和网页软件的界限，让它像一张纸一样自然。这种远大志向反过来激励着参与其中的团队成员。  

（00:22:13）：我可以继续列举。但归根结底，一支充满激情、内在驱动力强、带着“今天是我职业生涯的第一天，我好奇会发生什么”的态度的团队，才是文化的核心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you come up with these? What was the process to come up with company values? Because I know a lot of companies are like, "We should come up with these." How do you do that?
turns.zh: 你们是如何想出这些价值观的？制定公司价值观的过程是怎样的？因为我知道很多公司都说，“我们应该制定这些价值观。”但你们是如何做到的？

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: The secret is I hate corporate values. I've never resonated with them. And I'm fortunate, we're fortunate enough, to have a lot of really spectacular, experienced leaders in our corner. And I got hammered to the first year, two years on, "Josh, where are your values? How can your team operate without values?" And I always experienced them on the other end as almost corporate propaganda, these cliche fortune cookie, Panda Express-like, "You should care about the detail." It didn't resonate with me. And the thing that clicked was maybe a year and a half, two years into working, I just kept hearing the same things from the team. And I would do things like a year into someone joining, "How's it going? What's going well? What's not?" And I realized that there are some traits that define our team, extremely organically and naturally. No one told people what our values were. (00:23:51): Again, because I was this naive, ignorant 31-year-old being like, "Values are a corporate, late-stage capitalism creation," and just very, very hardheaded. And it was really special two years in, hearing from the team why they love The Browser Company, why they think we're doing ... Just the passion there. And then we challenged ourselves to what became a value. Well, if something about the five one-liners on the corporate webpage feels off, start by asking what could be in dream a little bit. And what I realized was, all of the statements people would say about what they loved about The Browser Company, what they thought defined the way we work, they reminded me of how I like to take road trips. I'm a big traveler. I'm a big fan of dropping in somewhere new and just exploring. And so we just had this "Aha!" Moment. Let's, instead of having a corporate landing page with five value titles and subtitles, let's write a manual for how to take a road trip. (00:24:54): So we wrote an essay called "Notes on Road Trips" that use this semi-biographical, but mostly fictional, story about a person and their father taking a road trip when they're a teenager, to tell the story of how we do things at The Browser Company. And share these values, but in a way that hopefully won't feel so propagandary and feel a little more, you're reading an essay. So I say that, again, not to say there's anything wrong with traditional values. I'm actually sure I'm going to get an earful for a lot of people that coach me and give me advice that I sounded too indignant on this podcast. But I'm pretty proud of that story because it was a great example of assuming you don't know. We were sure that corporate values were not for us. And then very organically without trying it turned out, "Wait! They run through this company in a pretty profound way. We should put some words around it, because it's happening whether or not we like it, or say it is or not."
turns.zh: 秘诀在于我讨厌那些企业价值观。我从未对它们产生共鸣。幸运的是，我们团队有很多非常出色、经验丰富的领导者。在我工作的头两年里，他们不断催促我：“乔希，你的价值观在哪儿？团队没有价值观怎么运作？”我一直觉得这些价值观更像是企业的宣传口号，像那些老掉牙的福袋语录，比如“你应该关注细节”。它们根本无法引起我的共鸣。直到工作两年半后，团队不断向我反馈同样的问题，我才有所领悟。比如，新人入职一年后，我会问：“进展如何？哪些方面进展顺利？哪些方面还需要改进？”这时我意识到，团队自然而然地形成了某些特质。根本没人告诉他们这些价值观是什么。（00:23:51）：说真的，我当时还是个31岁的愣头青，觉得“价值观是资本主义晚期企业的产物”，所以特别固执。两年后，听团队讲述他们热爱The Browser Company的原因，发现这些热情源自团队的价值观，这真是令人惊喜的时刻。当时我们在挑战自己，试图提炼出公司的核心价值观。但当我看到公司官网上的五条价值观标语时，总觉得哪里不对劲，于是决定放开思路。如果团队能畅想出理想的价值观，那就顺其自然吧。后来我发现，大家对The Browser Company的喜爱之处，以及他们认为定义我们工作方式的特质，都让我联想到自己喜欢公路旅行的经历。我是个狂热的旅行爱好者，喜欢随意探索新地方。于是我们灵光一现：与其在公司官网上列出五条价值观标题和副标题，不如写一篇关于公路旅行的指南。（00:24:54）：于是我们写了一篇名为《公路旅行笔记》的文章，通过半自传半虚构的故事，讲述一个少年和父亲的公路旅行，来诠释我们在The Browser Company的做事方式。用这种方式传递价值观，既不显得生硬，又像在读一篇散文。我这么说，并不是否定传统价值观。我知道很多人会批评我在这个播客上显得过于愤怒。但我对这个故事很自豪，它完美诠释了先假定自己无知的智慧。我们原以为企业价值观不适合我们，但最终却自然而然地发现，它们以深刻的方式贯穿于整个公司。既然它们无论我们是否承认、是否说出口，都在影响着我们，那我们就应该用文字将其具象化。

turns.zh: 好的。太棒了。这真的很有帮助。正如你们所见，我在Twitter上征集了提问，现在收到了大量问题。大家对你们的运作方式有很多疑问。最常见的问题来自Ched Khan，他的提问获得了最多点赞。是关于招聘的，基本上你们成功说服了世界上最优秀的一些人才加入Browser Company。比如你刚才提到的，你们甚至把Chrome的开发者招来了，现在让他专注于Arc项目。你们到底做了什么，能让这些优秀人才加入？因为大家都想向你们学习、模仿你们的做法。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Thank you for that question and for all the legs. I will admit, this is also a fairly awkward one to ask. I actually just came from an interview with a candidate and they asked me a fairly similar question. And I said, "You know what? You should go ask the people that work here. It's not me. I don't know why they ultimately join." But what I will tell you is, the intentionality, which is another secret, sharing a lot of secrets. This one will probably get me in trouble. I don't care about web browsers. I've never cared about web browsers. I never wanted to build a web browser. If you had told me a decade ago that I'd be working on a desktop first web browser at 32, "I'd say what in my career went horribly wrong?" The origin story of this company was Hursch, who I met when I was 20. We started a company together. Lots of mistakes, a lot of successes, a lot of growing pains and figured out who we are. And a decade later we were still friends, we went to each other's weddings. (00:29:10): We'd worked in all these different industries and different-stage companies and we just realized, "You know what? There are a lot of ideas that get us really excited. There are a lot of shapes and sizes." But as we were nostalgic for looking back on the decade prior, it was groups of people and moments in time with those people that were our best memories. And so, what Hursch and I decided, long before the company started was, we want to build a company, but we want to build a company where we feel like we can hire whoever we want. And I don't mean whoever we want in terms of who would dare say no. But we want to work on something where the greatest minds in our industry and adjacent would want to work on that prompt in a hypothetical sense. And then build an organization, build a team where we can work in the way that, after a decade of trying on a bunch of hats and ways of doing things and metrics this and [inaudible 00:30:04], we could do what was right for us. (00:30:06): And so, where we went to with a new web browser, let alone a web browser as a new form of computing, which is our true aspiration, to build an internet here. You can look up the internet computer YouTube video on our Browser Company YouTube page. But our ambition's even higher than a web browser. The intention of that is, we just want to go hire our favorite people that we know and don't know and build a team that, we'll never get bored working with this crew, because of how incredible they are and how humble they are. And so, when you think about it like that, I as the CEO as notionally the head of product, I view our product as our team. And I know a lot of companies say that. I actually think they probably all mean it. I don't think anyone's being disingenuous, but we really meet it. It is the genesis of this company. (00:30:55): It is not a new web browser. It is, let's build the dream team, our dream team. And let's build a way of working that is really fun for us and really speaks to our values. And let's go find people that resonate with that. And that trickles down to everything we do, whether it's our policy about this or the way we do that. I'll give you one example. Our goal of interviews is to convince people not to join The Browser Company. If I have an interview with someone, I don't pitch them and say, "What do you want to ask me? Anything you want? I'll be super honest, most people shouldn't want to work here." So I think it all starts with us viewing our product as the company, as the team, not Arc itself. And then, I think being self-aware, that that's how I think that's how we think. (00:31:43): But again, flying back things that I've heard, we have been fortunate. We've hired a lot of really remarkable people, especially on paper and especially off. I mean, all around. I'll just give a couple examples to share one thing that I've heard. A few recent hires, we hired someone named Darren who, as I mentioned, he co-created the first prototype of Chrome and then ran it for 16 years. I think hundreds if not thousands of people reported to him. He joined the Browser Company as an IC. We just hired a woman named Tara. She was on the original Paper by 53 team, one of my most inspiring products at the beginning of my career. Most recently she was actually, I believe, Senior SVP of product at Vimeo and a senior director of engineering. She joined our engineering team as an IC. We just hired someone named Peter Vidani. When I was 20 building consumer social software, he was the coolest, most impressive person. He was the first designer at Tumblr. Ran the design team at Tumblr for seven years and the most recently was SVP of design at Slack. Joined the team as an IC designer. (00:32:48): And though that sounds like I'm bragging, the thing that was really interesting and perplexing to us was, these are people that have made a lot of money, that have had really fancy titles, that have worked on transformative projects. Why are they joining this team? And I think something that people show up to The Browser Company with is, in addition to heartfelt intensity, this aspiration that their work at The Browser Company will come to define their careers. And that's coming from people that have done really remarkable things, by all accounts. (00:33:54): A very kind culture. I think if you've been doing this for a decade plus, your intolerance for bullshit is very, very low. And so, by no means do I think we're perfect. I don't think everyone shows up The Browser Company saying, "If I'm not on the equivalent of the early iPhone team, I'm going to be bummed." And I think that's carried forward to this tumbleweed of people saying, "[inaudible 00:34:23]. That's where I'm going to finally do the equivalent of building the iPhone." turns.zh:
感谢你的这个问题，也感谢大家的支持。我得承认，这个问题确实有点难以启齿。其实我刚结束与一位求职者的面试，他们问了我一个类似的问题。我当时回答：“你知道吗？你应该去问这里的员工。这事儿不归我管。我也不知道他们为什么最终选择加入。”但我可以告诉你的是，我们的用心经营——这也是个不为人知的秘密——很可能会给我带来麻烦。我对浏览器毫无兴趣，从来就没对浏览器感兴趣过，也从未想过要开发浏览器。如果十年前有人告诉我，32岁的我会先开发一款桌面浏览器，我会问：“我职业生涯哪儿出问题了？” 这家公司的起源故事，要从我20岁时结识的赫施说起。我们一起创办了公司。经历了诸多挫折与成功，克服了成长的阵痛，最终找到了自己的定位。十年后的今天，我们依然是朋友，还参加了彼此的婚礼。（00:29:10）我们曾在不同行业、不同发展阶段的公司工作过，回首往事时发现，留在记忆中最深刻的，始终是与那些人共度的时光。于是，我和赫施早在公司创立前就决定：我们要建立一家公司，但要确保能自由聘请心仪之人。我们所说的自由，不是指谁敢拒绝我们，而是指能吸引业内顶尖人才参与的公司。然后，我们要打造一个组织和团队，让成员能以十年间尝试过各种角色、方法和指标（还有[00:30:04不可闻]）后，最终找到适合自己的工作方式。（00:30:06）至于开发新浏览器，更不用说将浏览器作为全新计算形式——这才是我们的终极愿景——我们要打造互联网。我们可以在浏览器公司的YouTube页面观看“互联网计算机”视频。但我们的雄心远不止浏览器。我们真正的目标是，招募业内内外最优秀的人才，组建一支团队。与这些才华横溢、谦逊低调的伙伴共事，我们永远不会感到厌倦。因此，作为首席执行官兼名义上的产品负责人，我们将产品视为团队本身。我知道很多公司都这么说，但我相信他们是真心实意的。我们确实做到了这一点，这就是公司的根源。（00:30:55）这不是新浏览器，而是要组建梦想团队，打造属于我们的梦想团队。建立真正令我们乐在其中的工作方式，践行我们的价值观，并寻找与之共鸣的人。这理念渗透到我们的一切行动中，无论是招聘政策还是工作方式。我举个例子：我们的面试目标是说服候选人不要加入浏览器公司。如果有人来面试，我不会推销公司，说：“你想问什么？随便问。我实话实说，大多数人都不该来这里工作。” 所以一切都始于我们将产品视为公司、视为团队，而非Arc本身。然后，保持自我认知，清楚自己的定位，这才是关键所在。
嗯，我觉得我们就是这么想的。（00:31:43）但说回来，说些我亲耳听到的事。我们很幸运。我们招到了很多非常出色的人才，特别是那些在纸面上和实际表现都极为优秀的人。我是说全面来讲。我举几个例子，分享一下我听到的故事。最近新招的几个人，有个叫达伦的，正如我提到的，他参与了Chrome的首个原型开发，并管理了16年。我想有成百上千的人向他汇报工作。达伦加入浏览器公司时是独立贡献者（IC）。还有个叫塔拉的女士。她曾参与53 Paper团队的开发，这是我职业生涯初期最受启发的产品之一。最近她刚从Vimeo离职，之前她是Vimeo的产品高级副总裁兼工程总监，现在加入我们的工程团队担任IC设计师。还有个叫彼得·维达尼的，在我20岁开发消费级社交软件时，他是最酷、最令人印象深刻的人。他是Tumblr的首位设计师，负责Tumblr设计团队7年，最近刚从Slack离职，担任设计副总裁。现在加入我们团队担任IC设计师。（00:32:48）虽然听起来我像是在吹嘘，但真正有趣又令人困惑的是，这些人赚了很多钱，拥有很高的头衔，参与过变革性的项目。为什么他们会加入我们的团队？我认为人们加入浏览器公司时，除了满腔热忱，还有一个愿景——希望在浏览器公司的工作能定义他们的职业生涯。这话出自那些做过非凡成就的人之口。最重要的是，我们意识到，要让这样的人加入并怀着这样的愿景，就必须提供一些东西：令人振奋的抱负、充分授权让他们按照自己的方式为团队贡献力量，以及真正信任和赋权他们。（00:33:54）这是一种非常友善的文化。我觉得如果你从事这行十多年了，对胡说八道的容忍度会非常低。所以，我绝不认为我们是完美的。我不认为每个人加入浏览器公司时都会说：“如果我不能加入类似iPhone早期团队的项目，我会很失望。”但我认为总体来说，赫什和我，以及早期团队的每个成员，都怀着让浏览器公司成为产品本身的愿景。我认为这种精神延续到了现在这些人，他们说：“[00:34:23未听清]。这就是我最终要打造类似iPhone的产品的机会。”我们都知道这可能实现不了，但这种“我想再试一次”的心态会一直延续下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That tumbleweed is, I think a big part of it is, once you get amazing people, more amazing people want to join. So I think that's very much helpful. Something else this resonates a lot with is, just the mission of a company is such a powerful tool for pulling people in, the best people. I've seen that a lot with founders. If they have a meaningful mission, it's so much easier to hire, versus not. And clearly you're really good at sharing that vision and mission. And then you also have a really interesting mission and vision. I think there's also, you're just a charismatic founder and that helps a lot too. And you're a great storyteller.
turns.zh: 莱尼，我觉得吸引优秀人才的一个重要因素是，当你汇聚了杰出人才后，更多优秀的人会慕名而来。因此，我认为这非常有助于吸引人才。还有一点让我深有共鸣的是，一个公司的使命是吸引顶尖人才的强大工具。我在创业者身上经常看到这一点。如果他们有意义的使命，招聘就容易得多，不然就难上加难。显然，你非常善于传递这种愿景和使命感。而且你的使命和愿景本身就非常引人入胜。我认为你也是一位极具魅力的创业者，这一点也起到了关键作用。你讲故事的能力也堪称一绝。

turns.en: Well, the other thing I want to add Lenny is, again putting myself in the listener, I imagine a lot of what I just said probably sounded a little bit ... Could come off, if you don't know me and you don't, as a little bombastic or a little again romantic. Very tactically, I'll give you something that was just who we are, but I think has helped contribute to this tumbleweed. From the very first person we hired, we celebrated them publicly. The fact that they joined. And in a very heartfelt way, telling you about them as a person and what they did. Long before we had anyone that anyone would've heard of before working at The Browser Company, just because it was earnest, we were really proud. Again, if you think of our original mandate as building the companies, the product, when our first designer joins, we want to tell everyone about it. That's a product launch. That is the product launch. (00:35:57): And then, whenever we ship something, we go out of our way to celebrate the people that worked on it publicly. I think there's a CEO-hero worship sometimes in Silicon Valley. I do very little at the company. Or sorry. I do very little as it relates to the thing people fall in love with Arc. I do a lot for The Browser Company, but I don't make Arc. I didn't make Peek. And again, that's just who we are, which is, "Alexandre. She killed me! Look at how cool this is!" because it's earnest and it's honest to who we are. And then I think it creates this reinforcing cycle of you're someone that's done something incredible, which is, "I'm going to be celebrated. They truly want me here. I'm going to be recognized for the work that I do. (00:36:39): It's not going to just accrue to this like CEO figurehead who everyone thinks is some genius visionary. And so again, by no means are we perfect. By no means do I think we get it right all the time. But, because it's such an authentic expression of who we are and what we were trying to do, I think we do little micro implementations like that, that ladder up to that principle I got so excited about but are as simple as someone tweets about some animation. They're like, "Woo! This was fun." Tag Sherry. Sherry made that, Sherry's incredible. And you don't see that that much in Silicon Valley. You see corporate blog posts and the CEOs more than anyone else. That's probably why you don't have CEOs on the podcast, because you don't want ... You know this Lenny. That is why that's your policy. You don't want to hear from the CEOs. They're not the ones building the product. You want to hear from the people actually doing it. That's why I love this podcast.
turns.zh: 莱尼，我还想补充一点，站在听众的角度，我觉得我刚刚说的话可能听起来有点……如果你不了解我，可能觉得有点夸张或理想化。但说实话，这就是我们的真实写照。从我们聘请的第一个员工开始，我们就公开庆祝他们的加入，以真诚的方式讲述他们的故事和贡献。早在The Browser Company还默默无闻之前，我们就这样做了，因为这份真诚让我们倍感自豪。再说回我们的初始使命——打造公司和产品。当我们的首位设计师加入时，我们会向全公司宣布。这就是产品发布会。（00:35:57）每次发布新成果时，我们都会公开表扬参与其中的团队成员。硅谷有时会把CEO捧得神话般高大。但我其实在公司里做得很少。或者说，我在Arc这个产品上投入甚少。我为The Browser Company做了大量工作，但Arc不是我创造的。Peek也不是我的功劳。归根结底，这就是我们的本色——“亚历山大！她太棒了！看看这有多酷！”因为这份真诚和坦率契合了我们的本性。然后我认为这形成了一个良性循环：当你创造了非凡的成果，就会得到表扬，他们真心希望你留下，认可你的工作成果。（00:36:39）这不是CEO作为万能天才的神话化形象。再次强调，我们绝非完美。我也绝非总能做对。但正因为这份真诚地表达了我们的本色和初衷，我们才会做出这样微小的努力，比如推特上某个动画被点赞，大家会说：“哇！太有趣了。”标注雪莉。雪莉做的，雪莉太棒了。在硅谷你很少看到这种情景。那里充斥着企业博客和CEO的自拍照。这或许就是你不邀请CEO上播客的原因——你不想……莱尼，你懂的。这就是你的原则。你不想听CEO空谈，他们又不是产品创造者，你想听实干家发声。这就是我喜欢这个播客的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. That's right. Thank you. I'd say just hearing everything you're saying, The Browser Company sounds like an incredible place to work. I could see why people want to go work. It's pretty simple. You touched on being public and sharing everything that's going on. And that's another area I wanted to spend a little time on. You guys are very transparent about what's going on and inside the company. You bring cameras into the board meetings. I watched a half-hour meeting you had with your head of design talking about a project that's behind scheduling. You're trying to figure out how do we get this out the door. You just share actual things you all are doing within the company, publicly. And I'm curious just, why did you start doing that? What have you seen as a good or bad that has come from that? Is there anything you've shared that maybe you regret like "Oh, maybe we shouldn't have put that out there." What's been your experience with that?
turns.zh: 没错。没错。谢谢。听了你刚才说的一切，我觉得The Browser Company听起来确实是个非常棒的工作场所。我能理解为什么人们都想去那里工作。这很简单。你提到要公开透明，分享公司内部的一切动态。这也是我特别想深入探讨的领域。你们对公司内部运作非常开放透明，甚至在董事会会议上也会带摄像机拍摄。我看过你们和设计主管开会的半小时片段，讨论一个进度落后的项目，大家都在想办法如何尽快完成。你们公开分享公司内部的真实情况，我很好奇，你们为什么要这样做？从中获得了哪些积极或消极的反馈？有没有分享过后又后悔的事情，比如“哎呀，或许我们不该把这件事公之于众”？你们在这方面的经验如何？

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Why don't I start with the regret. It's not yet a regret, but the thing that I wonder ... Because this is very much ... I may have hopefully spoken with a lot of earnest passion to some of the questions before. This is one that I would really characterize as a prototype. We really have a prototype-driven culture. And this is one that I'd put high on the list of, "Maybe we'll regret this later." And specifically what I hope is that, I'm uncomfortable putting myself too central in our story. But, naturally, when you're doing storytelling publicly, there's a gravitational pull for the CEO and the founders to be at the center of that. And so, sometimes even this morning, we had our best-performing YouTube video ever. The first one that really broke out of people that already follow us. And it's a reaction video in classic YouTube form to MKBHD talking about our product for the first time. (00:39:13): And I honestly watched it right before this again, and I was like, "What the fuck am I doing? What are we doing? Why am I trying to become a YouTuber?" So, to be totally honest, I don't regret anything yet. But I wonder if we could take this too far? So if anyone's listening, if you see us starting to take this too far, especially as it relates to me, we want to hear about it, because that's keeping me up. But I do think the intentions are pure and earnest, which are ... And another thing that defines people that have joined The Browser Company, in addition to wanting to do the work that defines their careers, is I would characterize it as a little bit of hopelessness, maybe feeling jaded, questioning this industry that they've worked on or products that they've worked on and wanting to rediscover. But, at the end of the day, we are a group of idealists, of optimists, wanting to rediscover what we fell in love with when we were kids, whether it's the part of our craft or the potential of technology, the internet and software. (00:40:19): And, as part of that, I would view Arc and the Browser Company as an experiment in we can do it. Better is possible. And as we were thinking about better as possible, rediscovering what we love and believe in deep down and trying to express it in the world, one of it related to trust. I remember when I was a teenager using the internet for the first time and early on to college, just the hopefulness of what was possible, and the belief that these people building these tools, they were like heroes to me. Not just the leaders, but the teams, the companies, the brands. And somewhere along the way, I'm not blaming a single company, I'm not even saying that anyone did anything wrong, but culturally ... I was a sociology major. Culturally, we have lost trust in tech companies and in tech brands. (00:41:10): And so, building in public showing you our meetings, uncomfortably so, is an act in, "If we were them, why should they trust us? Why should anyone trust us?" We have your most sensitive personal data. We have your most sensitive professional data. Why should you trust us if we've had our trust broken again and again? And I think our hypothesis in this prototype, in this experiment is, we can have the best privacy policy in the world, but at the end of the day, again, it's just people behind the screen. And so, even if I think about ... I haven't done interviews like this, because I worry that if you don't know me, I come off the wrong way. (00:41:51): A lot of people tend to. I've noticed a lot of friends in my life that I know them behind the scenes, but the way that people perceive them publicly here don't know them. They interpret it the other way, because there's not that trust. And so our bet is that if you get to know us, Nash, Dina, me Hursch, and you really feel like you get to know us as person and all of our imperfections, we're average looking, we're average to all that stuff. Then when you see that we're asking for a permission, you might trust it is because we want to make you feel a certain way that's better. And if not ... I'll say someone tweeted something yesterday, who apparently we didn't earn the trust yet and they haven't gone to know us. And their interpretation of what we were doing was the worst possible interpretation you could [inaudible 00:42:40]. And, at first honestly, I felt a bit of anger, like, "Who was this person on a Thursday just saying we're doing X and Y?" And then I realized, "You know what? I'd have the same feeling because of the experiences I've had with technology in the past five to 10 years." (00:42:53): And so, the intention with these the building and public experiments are radical trust building. Not radical transparency, we can't share everything, but radical trust building. You get to know us as humans and I worry that we'll regret that, and that it could potentially turn into, "Oh, they're trying to be internet celebrities that they're so important, they should share everything because ... Thank you, them, for gracing us with their opinions." It's not the intention and it feels worth taking that risk. But that's the intentionality behind it.
turns.zh:
或许我该从后悔说起。这还算不上后悔，但我确实在思考……因为这事太重要了……我可能曾满怀热情地探讨过其中一些问题。这次可以说是典型的原型驱动文化案例。我把它列入了"未来可能会后悔"的清单之首。具体来说，我不愿把自己过度置于故事的中心，但当你公开讲述公司故事时，CEO和创始人总会不自觉地成为焦点。比如今天早上，我们的YouTube视频创下了新纪录——首次突破现有粉丝群体。这是一段MKBHD首次谈论我们产品的反应视频。（00:39:13）我刚刚又看了一遍，心里直犯嘀咕："我到底在搞什么鬼？我们这是要干嘛？我干嘛要当网红？"说实话，目前我还没后悔什么。但我担心我们是否做得太过了。所以，如果有听众发现我们越界了，尤其是涉及我的部分，我们希望能听到反馈，因为这让我夜不能寐。不过我相信初衷是纯粹而真诚的——除了想从事定义职业生涯的工作外，加入The Browser Company的人还带有几分无奈，可能是对所在行业或产品感到厌倦，渴望重新探索初心。归根结底，我们是一群理想主义者、乐观主义者，想要重拾童年时对技术、互联网和软件的热爱。（00:40:19）在这过程中，我们将Arc和The Browser Company视为一次实验，证明我们能做到更好。当我们追寻更好的可能性时，重新发现深藏心底的热爱与信仰，并试图将其展现于世。这其中与信任息息相关。我记得十几岁初次接触互联网时，对技术的潜力充满希望，觉得那些开发工具的人简直是英雄——不只是领导者，还有团队、公司和品牌。但不知何时起，我不怪任何特定公司，也不认为有人做错了什么，但从文化层面……我曾是社会学专业出身。文化层面上，我们对科技公司和科技品牌的信任已然丧失。（00:41:10）因此，公开分享我们的会议过程，坦然面对质疑："如果我们是他们，又怎会信任我们？又怎能让别人信任我们？"我们掌握着用户最敏感的个人数据和职业信息。若我们一次又一次辜负信任，又怎能期望人们信任我们？我认为这次原型实验的核心假设是：即便我们制定了全球最完备的隐私政策，最终归根结底，还是要靠背后的人来兑现承诺。（00:41:51）说到这，我很少接受这类采访，因为担心陌生人会误解我。（00:42:03）我注意到，现实中认识我的朋友们对我的看法和公众认知相差甚远。
了解我们。他们会用另一种方式解读这一切，因为信任感不足。所以我们的赌注是，如果你能真正了解我们——纳什、迪娜、我赫尔施，还有你——了解我们作为个体的所有缺点，我们长相普通，性格也普普通通。当你看到我们请求许可时，你或许会相信这是因为我们想让你感受到更好的体验。如果不是这样……我要说昨天有人在推特上发了些言论，显然他们还没建立起对我们的信任，也没有深入了解我们。他们对我们行为的解读简直糟糕透顶（00:42:40）。我一开始确实有些生气，比如“周四那个人凭什么说我们在做这个那个？”但后来我意识到，“说实话，我可能也会有同样的感受，毕竟过去五到十年里我在科技领域的经历太糟糕了。” （00:42:53）所以，这些公开实验的核心是建立信任，不是追求透明——我们不可能分享一切——而是建立信任。你要了解我们作为普通人，我担心人们会因此误解，认为我们想成为网络红人，自视过高，就该无所不露。“感谢你们大方地分享你们的看法。” 这绝非我们的初衷，但这种风险值得一试。这就是背后的初衷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really interesting insight. It makes a lot of sense for a browser to find that so important, to build that trust.
turns.zh: 这真是个很有意思的见解。对于浏览器来说，重视并建立这种信任感是完全说得通的。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: I haven't done podcast interviews, I haven't done this. I really like you. I really like the feeling of your conversations, the intentions behind them, the warmth, even your intro music is a friendly jig. So, I mean, it's a great example, where I think it's one of the most wonderful things about the podcasting medium is I've had you in my ear for a year and the people on your show and you feel a sense of trust in you and your intentions here. And your intentions both in this interview, in terms of what you're trying to do for listeners. To some extent your show, and the warmth that you bring to it and the perception I have as a human being ... We've never met. We've maybe DM'd briefly, maybe five messages exchanged. But I feel like I know you and that makes me trust you. And so, in many ways this podcast, at a meta level's an inspiration for it.
turns.zh: 我从未参与过播客采访，也没有做过这类事。我真的很欣赏你。我很喜欢你谈话时的感觉，你背后的初衷，你传递的温暖，甚至你的开场音乐都是一首友好的吉格舞曲。所以，我觉得这是一个很好的例子，我认为播客这种媒介最棒的地方之一，就是我已经听你的节目一年了，节目中的人和你的节目本身，都让我对你和你的初衷充满信任。无论是这次采访，还是你为听众所做的努力。在某种程度上，你的节目，以及你带来的温暖感，还有我对你的印象……我们从未见过面。我们可能简短地互发过五条消息，但我感觉我了解你，这让我信任你。所以，在很多方面，播客在宏观层面上给了我灵感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel the same way in reverse. You made this point about being worried about being two front and center for your company. I have the same exact feeling. Even though my newsletter's called "Lenny's Newsletter," I only named it that because that was the default recommendation when I was signing up for Substack. I didn't want to be this, "I know it all. Come to me. Welcome to my know-it-all place." I really dislike that. And that's why I created this community that lives along the side, where people can help each other, because I'm not going to have all answers. And so, I've had to lead into that. "All right, people." They want a person to help them understand what's going on, learn about ... And in your videos you do a great job highlighting other people. I was watching your board meeting video and it's like, "Here's all team members coming along. Here they come. How are you doing?" So, anyway. All that to say, you're doing a great job finding the balance.
turns.zh: 我对此感同身受。你提到担心在公司中成为焦点。我也有同样的感受。尽管我的通讯叫做“Lenny's Newsletter”，但我之所以这么命名，只是因为我在Substack上注册时，这是默认的推荐名称。我不想成为那种“我无所不知，请来找我。欢迎来到我的万事通之地”的人。我真的很讨厌这种感觉。所以，我创建了这个社区，让人们可以在边栏互助，因为我不可能掌握所有答案。因此，我必须引导大家：“好的，各位。”他们希望有人帮助他们理解正在发生的事情，学习相关知识……而你在视频中很好地突出了其他人。比如，我看了你的董事会会议视频，里面说：“所有团队成员都来了。他们来了。你好吗？”总之，所有这些都说明你找到了平衡点。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Oh, thank you. You as well.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢你。你也一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate it. You talked about storytelling, and you mentioned that you have a whole bunch of odd teams at The Browser Company. One of them is a storytelling team. And that actually explains, I think, how you're so good at making these really amazing videos, because making great videos is hard. Can you just talk about some of these odd teams that you have, that probably other companies don't?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你提到故事讲述，你提到The Browser Company有许多奇特的团队。其中一个就是故事讲述团队。这实际上解释了为什么你能制作出如此精彩的视频，因为制作优质视频并不容易。你能谈谈你拥有的这些奇特团队吗？其他公司可能没有这样的团队？

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: One of the other things that, hopefully, you're picking up in this interview, so far, is we are a very prototype-driven culture. It goes back to the "assume you don't know" ethos. We try a lot of experiments, and we try them related to product features related to how we work together, related to the stories we tell. So, this isn't a category of, "I'm not sure it's going to work, but we're trying it," and it seems to be working so far, at least for us. What Lenny's referencing is, we have a handful of teams. I'll pick two just as an examples. We have a membership team and we have a storytelling team. And though you probably recognize or are obviously familiar with those terms, those aren't historically startup orgs, or startup disciplines and teams. And let me tell you about the intention behind both. (00:46:16): Membership. Membership was, when I was at Facebook, the most impressive thing to me about how Facebook built product was their user research team. Shout out to Lowie and Jane. I don't know why you'd be listening to this podcast, but you deeply inspired me when we were at Facebook together. They had the most incredible team of user researchers. And it always felt odd to me. And this isn't Lowie and Jane's fault. Actually, in fact, they suffered from this. That user research almost felt like a service organization, relative to product engineering design. There'd be a PM. The PM would get assigned a researcher and the PM got to decide how to use the researcher, and ask them what to do and ask them questions. But seeing the potential for when you really get to know the people that you are building for, that you're serving, at a really deep way, it is extraordinary. How do you build product any other way? (00:47:09): And so, we took that to the extreme at The Browser Company, which we said, "Let's not think of it as customer support, customer service, customer success, user research. Those are just business terms. Those are just industry terms." At the end of the day, what we're saying is if there is a human being, from the moment they touch our software or our products for the first time, to, if they have it last, we need to have a deep, genuine, ongoing relationship with them. (00:47:36): And on day one, that may be air quote, "customer success." "How do I use this thing?" On day 37, that might be, "I have a bug. Do you mind helping me fix it?" And on day 58, that may be, "Hey, we're shipping the mobile app soon. What do you want from mobile? What do you want on your phone?" Other companies view that as different orgs and disciplines. We view that as, there are a bunch of people at the other end of this that we are serving from the moment they touch our product the first time. Let's own that relationship full stack and think about it holistically. And so that's the membership team. (00:48:07): On the storytelling side, very similar, different type of person. Again, we're a humanistic the company. So, the theme here is the people on the company, the people at the other end. So if the membership team takes people from the moment they touch our product for the first time to the last, the storytelling team is about people we don't have the privilege of serving yet. They don't use Arc, they don't know what Arc is. That could be an investor, air quote, "investor relations." That could be members of the press, air quote, "PR." That could be just people out in the world, air quote, "marketing" and one-day sales. But at the end of the day, it's telling our story to people. It's telling our story to people and thinking about that holistically in full stack. (00:48:47): So that's how we think about teams is, we start with first principles asking, what are we really trying to do here? And what is the most direct way to manifest that, even if it's not how other people do it? In practice, one of the benefits of that is I do think it leads to certain pieces of content. For example, that people go, "Oh, wow! I've never seen that before." But again, I think anyone's capable of this. I think we have an extraordinarily talented storytelling team and membership team, but I really think it's as simple as the intentionality of what is the team? What are their incentives? What are the disciplines on the team? Even hiring a video editor, for example, as a small company. But the video editor, not having make a TikTok account go viral. But think about it more holistically in terms of the people. (00:49:33): So, again, there's a lot that breaks down. There's a lot that's not going well about it. I have no idea how the scales, the 500 people ... Yeah. So this is not me saying this experiment is ultimately going to be a huge success, or right for everyone or even us at different times. But that was the intentionality of the membership team, the storytelling team and others. And even product management. We don't have PMs at the company. My title at Facebook was Product Manager. I love product management. But, we view it not as a team. We view it as a leader, a role on a project, on an effort. (00:50:07): And depending on the projects, different types of people should be a PM. So, we have a performance-related project going on where, of course, an infrastructure engineer should be that air quote, "PM." We have a product project, where actually I think someone from membership should be the PM, because ultimately, yes, we're building software product, but it is really about serving our members in a specific way, so we should have someone for membership be a PM. Again, as you can imagine, as is going through the heads of everyone listening, "That must break down in 18 ways?" Oh, it definitely does. And so I'm not promising one day it won't change. But again, continuous through the company is, assume you don't know. Start by asking what could be, and let's just try some things and see what happens.
turns.zh:
希望大家在这次访谈中能逐渐领会到，我们是一家极度重视原型驱动文化的公司。这种文化源于"假定你一无所知"的理念。我们尝试了大量实验——无论是产品功能创新、团队协作方式革新，还是叙事策略探索。这些尝试并非一时兴起的冒险，而是经过深思熟虑的探索。至少目前看来，这种方法对我们行之有效。

莱尼提到的两个团队为例：会员团队和叙事团队。这些术语或许听起来耳熟，但它们并非传统初创公司的组织架构或标准职能。接下来，我将详细解读两者的核心理念。

（00:46:16）：会员团队。Facebook时期最令我惊叹的是其用户研究团队——向洛维和简致敬。虽然我不知道你们为何收听这期播客，但我们共事期间你们深深启发了我。他们拥有令人惊叹的用户研究团队。然而这支团队常被视为服务型部门，相较于产品工程设计部门显得边缘化。项目经理分配研究员后，由PM决定如何使用研究成果，提出问题并获取反馈。但当你真正深入了解目标用户时，建立深度、真诚的持续关系将带来非凡价值。试问：还有哪种产品开发方式能超越这种思维？

（00:47:09）：因此，我们在The Browser Company将其推向极致："别把用户视为客户支持、客服或用户研究的对象——这些都是商业术语。" 从用户首次接触产品到最后离场，我们需要与他们建立深度、真诚、持续的关系。

（00:47:36）：第一天可能是被引号括起的"客户成功"时刻："如何使用这款产品？"；第37天可能是"我遇到了漏洞，能帮忙修复吗？"；第58天可能是"移动应用即将上线，你希望添加哪些功能？" 其他公司将这些视为不同部门或职能，而我们将其视为与产品另一端的用户建立全方位、整体性关系。这就是会员团队的使命。

（00:48:07）：叙事团队同样秉持人本主义理念。核心主题是面向用户的全生命周期服务：会员团队关注用户从首次接触到最后离场的全过程；叙事团队则专注于尚未有幸服务的群体——他们未使用Arc产品，不了解Arc；可能是投资者（引号中的"投资者关系"）；可能是媒体（引号中的"公关"）；可能是市场营销或一日销售。但归根结底，这关乎向世界讲述我们的故事。
全面地从全栈视角来看。（00:48:47）：所以我们对团队的思考方式是，从第一性原理出发，问问自己：我们真正想在这里做什么？最直接的实现方式是什么？即使这与其他人的做法不同，又有何妨？在实践中，这样做的好处之一是，我确实认为这能催生出一些独特的内容。比如，人们会惊呼：“哇！我从未见过这样的东西！” 但我认为任何人都能做到这一点。我认为我们拥有极具才华的讲故事团队和会员团队，但我认为关键在于明确团队的定位：他们的激励机制是什么？团队的纪律性如何？即便是在小公司招聘视频编辑也是如此。但关键在于更全面地考虑团队成员的特质。（00:49:33）：所以，再说一次，存在诸多挑战。很多方面进展不顺。我不知道如何衡量这500人的规模……是的。所以我不是说这个实验最终会取得巨大成功，或者适合所有人，甚至对我们自己在不同时期也适用。但这就是会员团队、讲故事团队和其他团队的初衷。甚至产品管理团队也是如此。我们公司没有产品经理。我在Facebook的头衔是产品经理。我热爱产品管理，但我们不把它视为一个团队，而是视为一个项目或努力中的角色。（00:50:07）：根据项目的不同，不同类型的成员应该担任产品经理。比如，我们正在进行一个与绩效相关的项目，在这种情况下，当然应该由基础设施工程师担任所谓的“产品经理”。而对于产品项目，我认为会员团队的人应该担任产品经理，因为归根结底，我们是在开发软件产品，但这实际上是为了以特定方式服务我们的会员，所以会员团队的人应该担任产品经理。当然，你可以想象，听众们肯定会想：“这肯定会出18个问题吧？” 哦，确实如此。我不保证未来某天情况不会改变。但公司的核心理念始终是：假设你一无所知。从可能发生的情况入手，尝试一些方法，看看结果如何。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Yeah. We've increasingly hiring people that at other companies may have a PM title. I'd say we have two to three right now, that could have a PM title at another company. I don't think we will have a pm organization, or a PM role, because again, we believe depending on ... turns.zh: 是的。我们越来越多地招那些在其他公司可能被称为PM的人。我觉得我们现在有两到三位，如果在其他公司，他们可能有PM头衔。我不认为我们会建立PM组织或PM角色，因为我们认为……如果你拆解PM的职责，我觉得任何我们招的人都能胜任。这真的取决于项目是什么，以及我们想做什么。我认为不变的是我们喜欢招多面手。暂时还没想到一个更讨喜的词，因为这个词本意就很讨喜……比如公司里有个叫丽贝卡的女士。（00:52:58）：丽贝卡曾是我们Cora公司用的数据科学家。她在麻省理工学院获得了行为心理学之类的博士学位。我可能记错了。但她在麻省理工学院拿了什么疯狂学位，然后在Stripe做过软件工程师。我是在看丽贝卡的简历时发现她的。丽贝卡身上有很多闪光点。她现在实际上在扮演PM角色。她在有效管理我们的多人团队。但见丽贝卡最棒的地方在于，她和公司里的其他人都有这样的心态：“我要把东西做出来，我会做任何需要做的事来实现我的目标。无论用什么动词，无论遵循什么纪律。” 这就需要在实践中和工作方法上都是多学科的人。这不是说我们不招PM，而是我们想招有多学科思维、把事情看作“我要把东西做出来”的员工。有时他们会扮演PM的角色，有时又会做其他事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This can be a really interesting story to follow. I've seen this journey a few times at different companies. What I find is a lot of times people that are good at other things like engineering or design, for a while, they're like, "Yep. We don't need PMs. I'll do the PM job." And then eventually they're like, "This sucks. I hate doing this stuff. I want to design. Leave me alone. I don't want to sit on a [inaudible 00:54:29] all day. I don't want to be in meetings." So eventually, it turns out, they're like, "Okay. Let's find someone to do this thing that loves it." And so that's one thing that happens. (00:54:36): The other thing I find is, I'm sure you've seen this, a lot of people are wary of PMs. They come in and they're like, "Here's what we're doing," and they're just adults process complexity. What I find is those are just bad PMs. If you have an awesome PM, everything just gets better. Everyone's happier, things move faster. So I think companies often get to that stage. And then also there's just career development stuff, eventually as you scale. It's like "What happened to my career path," and they're like, "All right. Well, we got to go on one road or another." It's hard to stay in this hybrid role. But I super respect the first principal's approach of let's just-
turns.zh: 这会是一个非常有趣的故事，我在不同公司见过很多这样的例子。我的发现是，许多擅长工程或设计等其他领域的人，一开始会觉得“没错，我们不需要产品经理，我来做产品经理的工作”。但最终他们会说：“这太糟糕了，我讨厌做这些事，我想设计，别来烦我，我不想整天坐在[不可听清的00:54:29]上开会。”所以最终，他们会说：“好吧，让我们找个热爱这份工作的人来做吧。”（00:54:36）：另外，我还发现，很多公司对产品经理持谨慎态度。他们一进来就说：“我们要这么做”，然后就只是在用成人思维处理复杂问题。我的经验是，那些糟糕的产品经理会把事情搞砸。优秀的产品经理能让一切变得更好，每个人都更快乐，事情进展更快。所以我认为公司通常会经历这个阶段。然后，随着规模扩大，职业发展问题也会出现。比如“我的职业路径怎么了？”，然后公司会说：“好吧，我们必须选择一条路走下去。” 要保持这种混合角色很难。但我非常尊重第一位首席执行官的做法——就放手让他们去——

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: And, for what's worth, Lenny. I think you're almost, definitely right. And I think it will almost definitely happen with us. And again, this goes back to the "assume you don't know." The "assume you don't know," is try a prototype and then assume it's not going to work. So, even in my own experience, I remember getting to know Evan from Snapchat just enough to know how he talked about PMs at Snap. And it was, "We're never going to hire PMs at Snap. Everyone's a designer." And, I have no relationship with him anymore, but you can look, there are a lot of PMs at Snapchat. (00:55:37): So I know from my own experience with people that I respect from a product perspective that were indignant, they would never hire PMs, their organizations now have PMs. And that's probably for a really good reason. I would tell say also on our team, if any of our designers are listening, they'll tell you these, whatever you want to call it, "These verbs are taking up a lot of my time, and I do not have as much time to think and dream and design and do user research." And so, we're already feeling it breaking into our company. (00:56:04): I think the intentionality, whatever comes next, whatever it is, is leaders of the project should be picked for the projects, not because they're in a certain org at our company. And, if we ever hire people to do the PM role, we want them to think of themselves as people who make things and have lots of different disciplines and tools in their toolkit, not just the PM discipline. And, of course, even that could be wrong, and maybe in a year we cave. I got it totally wrong. We got it totally wrong. So, we'll see. But I would also, that that of all the things I shared on this podcast so far, this is probably the one I'll come crawling back to your podcast in a couple years, being, "Lenny, you were right. It all blew up!"
turns.zh: 还有，顺便说一句，Lenny。我觉得你几乎、肯定是对的。而且我认为这几乎肯定会在我们这里发生。这又回到了“假设你一无所知”的原则。“假设你一无所知”，就是先做个原型，然后假设它不会成功。就拿我自己来说，记得我认识Snapchat的Evan时，对他在Snapchat如何谈论产品经理的印象是：“我们永远不会在Snap雇佣产品经理，每个人都是设计师。” 我现在和他没有联系了，但你可以看看，Snapchat有很多产品经理。（00:55:37）：所以我从自己认识的在产品方面值得尊敬的人身上知道，他们曾愤然表示永远不雇佣产品经理，现在他们的组织里却有产品经理了。这很可能是有充分理由的。我要告诉我们团队，如果有设计师在听，他们会告诉你，这些“动词”占据了他们大量时间，而他们没有足够时间思考、梦想、设计和做用户研究。我们已经感受到这股力量在渗透我们的公司了。（00:56:04）：我认为无论接下来会发生什么，关键在于项目的领导者应该为项目而选，而不是因为他们在公司的某个部门。即使我们最终雇佣产品经理，我们也希望他们把自己视为能创造价值的人，拥有多种技能和工具箱，而不是仅限于产品经理这一种技能。当然，这也可能是错的，也许一年后我们会妥协。我完全想错了。我们完全想错了。所以走着瞧吧。但在迄今为止我在这个播客上分享的所有内容中，这可能是最有可能让我在几年后回到你的播客，说：“Lenny，你是对的。一切都爆发了！”的一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it's a fun experiment and Snap is a good example. Stripes another, where they waited a long time to hire their first PMs. And I think it's because their designers or engineers were just incredibly good at that element. And it was also very design-forward or very edge-forward, so they didn't need as much PM skill initially.
turns.zh: 不过这是一个有趣的尝试，Snap就是一个很好的例子。Stripe也是如此，他们很久才聘请了首位产品经理。我认为这是因为他们的设计师或工程师在产品经理角色上表现得极为出色。此外，Stripe的理念非常以设计为导向、前沿创新，因此最初并不需要过多依赖产品经理的技能。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: If I had to predict, I would predict that if we found that we were missing this discipline as a team, I think we would evolve Rebecca's team, which is technically the data team, and do something closer to a technical PM or data plus [inaudible 00:57:19] Again, it's all live, but the thought has even crossed our minds recently, that we may be wrong, and what org might we create if we need folks that have more of a background of [inaudible 00:57:29] like this.
turns.zh: 如果让我预测的话，我认为如果我们发现团队缺乏这种管理能力，我会考虑强化丽贝卡的团队——从技术层面来说，丽贝卡的团队就是数据团队。我们可能会让他们更接近技术产品经理或数据分析师的角色，再加上[00:57:19处语音不清]。当然这都还处于探索阶段，但最近我们确实在思考，我们是否可能做错了，如果需要具备更多相关背景的人才，我们又该组建怎样的团队呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited for the video of this discussion that might happen. It's also interesting, your PM that you mentioned, Rebecca is very data oriented. And then, the initial discussion we had around focus on feelings and that sort of thing. So, that's cool that you have this really interesting balance of people that are very data focused and then this, "Okay. But let's not obsess with that. What are the feelings we're trying to create?"
turns.zh: 我很期待这次讨论的视频回放。很有意思的是，你提到的丽贝卡确实非常注重数据。而我们最初讨论的焦点是关注用户感受之类的问题。所以，很棒的是，你团队里既有专注数据的人，又能说"好吧，但别太执着于此。我们到底想传递怎样的情感呢？"

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: Yeah. Because again, the point of optimizing for feelings is not hire people who make feelings. It's like Rebecca's title is Data Lead. She runs our data team. But, Rebecca's one of the most humanistic people I know. You meet her and you feel the warmth that you feel when you talk to you, and you ask her what she does outside of work. And so, it's not that data doesn't have a role. Actually I'd say, for better or worse, data is part of our practice. It's more about what's that top-level intentionality? What are we trying to do here? But, yeah. We have a lot of people that, data is either a noun they've had in their resume or it's been a part of their practice a lot in the past.
turns.zh: 是的。因为优化用户感受的关键不在于雇佣能制造情感的人才。丽贝卡的头衔是数据主管，她负责我们的数据团队。但她是我认识的最有人性的人之一。你见到她会感受到她给人的温暖，无论是聊天还是询问她工作之外的兴趣爱好。这并不是说数据没有作用，实际上，无论好坏，数据都是我们实践的一部分。关键在于顶层的战略意图是什么？我们到底想达成什么目标？不过确实，我们团队里很多人，要么在简历里写过数据相关的经历，要么过去在实践中大量运用过数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. One very tactical question with the storytelling team makes me think about Airbnb's video team. A lot of people are joking internally for years and years that the videos Airbnb put out in the early days accounts for half their market cap, because they're so good. And you're just like, "Oh, my God, I want to go on an Airbnb." They just make you feel so much and they're soul made. So, what is the makeup of your storytelling team? Because I imagine some companies maybe listening, like maybe we should do something like this on our team.
turns.zh: 太棒了。关于故事团队的一个很实际的问题让我想到了Airbnb的视频团队。多年来，内部大家一直开玩笑说，Airbnb早期推出的视频几乎占据了其市值的一半，因为那些视频太棒了。你会不由自主地想"天哪，我真想去Airbnb体验一把"。他们的视频能让人深深共鸣，充满灵魂。那么，你的故事团队由哪些成员组成？因为我想有些公司可能会听了之后想，在我们团队里也应该组建这样一个团队。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: We have a three-person storytelling team. It's run by a woman named Nash. There is a gentleman named Ellis, who is a ... Background, started as a reporter at The Verge. Maybe there was a publication before that. But I met him when he was a reporter at The Verge covering social media. And then he ran marketing strategy for Snapchat for seven years. And then we have a person named Josh Lee, who I actually met as an intern. He was an intern at Facebook as a designer, that an intern for me at the White House when I worked at the White House, and then decided that he was over product design and over design, and totally just jumped and be like, "I'm going to be a filmmaker," and has been making really fascinating indie films for a few years now. And he's our video editor on the team. (00:59:44): And it's so interesting. Nash's background, she had a brief stint at NBC. But again, you get to know her and she writes poems after hours and her dream is to write a fictional book. I mean, anyone that knows Nash, especially [inaudible 01:00:00] is just a force. A force. And the three of them, what's so interesting about them, which also relates to our design team ... One of the things I also found at Facebook is there was a tendency toward homogeneity. As you know, there's a stereotype of a Facebook PM for example, or a Google PM, the contrast between them and the way they work. And one of the things we also have purposely done on the storytelling team and otherwise, let's hire radically different archetypes. Ellis cannot be more different than Nash. Nash cannot be more different than Josh. There's some shared values, there's some shared beliefs, but they're very different. (01:00:35): Ditto on the design team. Our design team? They are all over the place in terms of who they are, what they've done, their sensibilities, their aspirations. And whether it's the storytelling team or the design team, that can be hard sometimes, just to be honest. It's a lot easier to say, "Hey, we're the Acme Co storytelling team, we're Acme Co design team. We hire designers like this and storytellers that." We hire people all over the place. We have an extremely diverse team, but in all senses of the word. But again, the no PM thing, it's not without flaws. I can see why a lot of large companies over time tend are like, "It's the Facebook way or no way," or "You're not good for here."
turns.zh: 我们的故事讲述团队由三人组成。团队负责人是名叫纳什的女性。还有一位叫埃利斯的男士，他曾在《The Verge》担任记者。或许他之前还有其他媒体经历，但我是在他为《The Verge》报道社交媒体时认识他的。之后，他在Snapchat担任了七年的营销策略主管。还有一位叫乔希·李的人，我最初是以实习生的身份认识他的。他曾在Facebook担任设计师实习生，在我白宫工作期间也曾为我做过实习。后来他决定放弃产品设计和设计工作，转而投身电影制作，过去几年一直在拍摄非常引人入胜的独立电影。他现在是我们团队的视频编辑。（00:59:44）：纳什的背景也很有趣。她曾在NBC短暂任职。但再深入了解她就会发现，她业余时间会写诗，她的梦想是写一部虚构小说。尤其是认识纳什的人都知道，她简直是个不容小觑的存在。三个人中，他们各自的特质最引人注目，这也与我们的设计团队息息相关……我在Facebook时发现，那里存在着同质化倾向。比如，人们对Facebook的产品经理（PM）或谷歌的产品经理存在刻板印象，比较两者的不同工作方式。我们故事讲述团队也有意招聘截然不同的成员。埃利斯与纳什截然不同，纳什又和乔希大相径庭。他们有一些共同的价值观和信念，但个性迥异。（01:00:35）：设计团队也是如此。我们的设计团队成员背景各异，经历不同，审美不同，抱负也各不相同。无论是故事讲述团队还是设计团队，有时确实会面临挑战。诚实地说，要想说"我们是Acme公司故事讲述团队，我们是Acme公司设计团队。我们招聘这样的设计师和这样的故事讲述者"，要比这复杂得多。我们团队成员背景多元，从各个方面来看都是如此。但同样，不设产品经理的模式也并非完美无缺。我能理解为什么许多大公司最终会坚持"要么照搬Facebook模式，要么另起炉灶"，或者"你不适合这里"。

turns.zh: 是啊。我记得自己职业生涯早期去Airbnb办公室时，看到墙上挂满了分镜图，当时就想：“我一定要来这里工作。”所以，我其实不太熟悉……我是说，我对Airbnb的视频和品牌营销很熟悉，简直太棒了，请原谅我这么说。但确实，我记得在那间办公室里走来走去，心想：“天哪！他们是在拍电影吗？我一定要[不清不楚 01:01:53]在这里工作。”

turns.zh: 真有意思你提到这个。想找的人可以去节目笔记里看看链接。但如果你在谷歌上搜索“白雪公主Airbnb”，实际上就能看到这些故事板。他们当时聘请了皮克斯的分镜师，绘制出房东和客人旅程的关键帧画面。这成为了整个策略的核心——让每个瞬间都尽可能令人惊喜。而这一切都源自《白雪公主》这部电影。你可以去了解一下。

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: For what it's worth, this is a great moment to share. All of the beliefs that I've shared here on behalf of our team, these aren't things that we just originally came up with. turns.zh: 说实话，现在分享这个故事再合适不过了。我代表团队分享的所有理念，都不是我们一时兴起想出来的。比如我职业生涯早期去Airbnb办公室时，看到墙上挂着《白雪公主》的故事板，这对我影响很大。甚至当你想到那个场景时，会发现其中的传承——比如当客人第一次打开房门时，我们要如何让他们感受到那种惊喜。所以我觉得这是一个绝佳的契机，让我们回顾那些灵感源泉，比如在Airbnb的那个日子，这些灵感逐渐渗透到我们如何优化用户体验的思考中。但这些灵感并非凭空产生，而是我们对行业观察的升华。这些成果离不开众多前辈和公司的推动，我们深感荣幸。

turns.zh: 希望如此吧。我强烈推荐一部纪录片《General Magic》。这是我看过的关于科技行业最棒的媒体作品之一，非常引人入胜。片中两种观点值得玩味：有些人看完后会感叹“天啊！真是错失良机”或将其视为悲剧；而我则会想：“要是有幸能组建那样一支团队该多好。”这部纪录片讲述的是iPhone问世前夕的General Magic公司，聚集了最传奇的技术人才团队。尽管从传统商业角度来看，它彻底失败了，但片中人物对往事的自豪、怀念和激情却令人动容。如今我在播客中谈论General Magic，证明了这些灵感的延续性。这对我个人而言，是情感深处的终极目标。要是我们能有这样的幸运，那无疑就是成功了。

turns.zh: 最后再说一句，我本想从Airbnb的故事叙述和电影制作元素的角度来谈谈这个话题。一个有趣的细节是，Airbnb早期有一段时间，产品经理被称为“制作人”，因为创始人曾说：“我们不想管理产品，我们想创造美好的体验”，就像电影制作人一样。这样的称呼持续了大约一年半。问题是，我们收到了很多艾美奖获奖制作人的求职申请，他们说：“哦，我想去Airbnb工作。”

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
turns.en: I know this podcast is about very tactical advice. So, one tactical piece of advice I'll give is, whether or not you like the idea of the storytelling team or something else, a byproduct of some of these experiments that we've found works really well is when you give something a new name, it sheds a lot of preconceived notions of what the thing should be. We found that even with product. So if you say you're building a browser history feature, then the benefit is everyone knows what you're talking about. And the downside is, everyone knows what you're talking about. And you show up with these preconceived notions of what it has to be. And so, if you go back again to revalue ask what could be ... In many ways the point of calling the team, the storytelling team or the membership team, or not having PMs as an organization ... All of this stuff isn't meant to be novelty for novelty's sake. It's meant to almost be a rhetorical tactic, to make people think truly first principles about what are we trying to do here? (01:06:00): And again, if at the end, producers are called PMs, that's fine. But I assume when it was called a producer, a much more intentionality was given to you communicating and talking and discussing, what does a producer do? What's their relationship with design? Because no one knew what the heck a producer was. And so, ultimately, that may have been failure in other ways. But that's one of the things we found tactically to be really helpful is, whether it's a product feature or a team, or whatever, give it a made up name just to really get to the root of what you're trying to do there. Or not borrow too much from wherever you worked before, whatever you've seen, popular media or whatever.
turns.zh: 我知道这个播客主要讲的是实用建议。所以，我给出的一个实用建议是：无论你是否喜欢故事叙述团队或其他模式，我们发现的一些实验副产品效果非常好。比如给某个功能起一个新名字，可以消除人们对其功能的先入之见。即使在产品领域也是如此。比如你说要开发浏览器历史记录功能，好处是大家都知道你在说什么，但坏处是大家也知道你在说什么，并且带着先入之见认为它必须是某种特定的东西。所以，再回过头重新评估：它能是什么样的？在很多方面，称团队为“故事叙述团队”或“会员团队”，或者在组织中不设产品经理……这些做法并非为了标新立异。它们更多是策略性的手段，目的是让人们真正思考：我们到底想做什么？（01:06:00）：再说一次，如果最后把“制作人”称为产品经理，那也可以。但我猜当时称他们为“制作人”时，更多是为了让团队更专注于沟通和讨论：制作人是做什么的？他们与设计的关系是什么？因为当时没人清楚“制作人”到底是什么。所以，最终这可能在其他方面导致了失败。但我们发现的一个实用策略是：无论是产品功能、团队还是其他方面，给它一个自创的名字，这样才能真正触及你想做事情的核心。或者不要过多借鉴你之前的工作经验、看到的案例、流行媒体等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it's very undo ... Like, you've got to undo it. It was-

turns.speaker: Josh Miller
